notes: User plans a large backyard BBQ with brisket, pulled-pork sandwiches (bun, coleslaw, pickles), burgers, hot dogs, and grilled pineapple. Sweet Baby Ray’s is a reliable favorite, especially with ribs, but is open to other sauces; Kansas City Masterpiece is currently an all-time favorite. Mac and cheese is a chosen side. Brisket plan: 10–12 lb whole packer, post-oak chips, 225°F smoker, trim fat/remove silver skin, Killer Hogs rub, and cook mainly to probe tenderness (often ~195–205°F), not merely 180°F. A typical whole packer generally takes ~10–14 hours. Pulled pork: boneless pork shoulder/Boston butt at 225–250°F, roughly 190–195°F for shreddability, preferably apple/cherry; hickory sparingly. User enjoys quick weeknight cooking on a new Weber gas grill and appreciates practical grilling, topping, side, sauce, and food-safety tips. Keep seasoned meat refrigerated unless briefly tempering; grilling guidance should specify 160°F for ground beef burgers.
trajectory: User is planning another backyard BBQ with ribs and brisket for friends. Side they chose: mac and cheese. Sauce: Sweet Baby Ray’s for ribs. Brisket plan: Low and Slow Smoked Brisket, using post oak wood chips, 225°F smoker, trimming excess fat and removing silver skin, then applying Killer Hogs BBQ Rub. Interested in beginner-friendly smoker setup, wood/flavor choices, rub pairing, meat prep, food safety, and tenderness tips. Ensure future guidance is accurate: brisket tenderness is determined mainly by cooking to probe tenderness (often ~195–205°F), not just 180°F; trimming and removing silver skin improve shape/even cooking but don’t directly make meat tender. Avoid recommending prolonged room-temperature resting of seasoned meat; refrigerate unless deliberately tempering briefly. For a typical 10–12 lb whole packer, cook time is usually closer to 10–14 hours depending on smoker, weather, and brisket.
